### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Ganimian, Ho, and Campos Quintero report Generalizability (G) and Decision (D) studies of classroom observations and Tripod-style student surveys that Enseñá por Argentina, a Teach for All affiliate in the Province of Buenos Aires, administered for its own formative purposes to roughly 100 novice teachers in 2014 and 2015, after a single one-hour rater training and with rater assignment driven by logistics rather than design. The paper's arithmetic is sound and unusually transparent: every generalizability coefficient, SEM, and teacher-effect SD in Tables 2 and 3, the Figure 1 curves, and the text's single-lesson coefficients (0 to 0.61, mean 0.39) regenerate exactly from the published variance components and equations, and the D-study increments the paper recommends (roughly 6 to 9 percentage points from a third clinical-practice lesson, about 8 from a third school-year occasion, with diminishing returns thereafter) hold. What the field should not take from the paper is its most quotable line, that these estimates are "comparable to those from research in high-income countries." The eight observation coefficients pool three different definitions of error. When the same peer scored both of a teacher's lessons (relative coefficients 0.75 and 0.75), the peer's stringency is confounded with the teacher's true score; in the per-coach studies (0.34 to 0.66, each clinical-practice fit resting on roughly four or five teachers), coach stringency is held fixed and drops out of the error; only the different-peer-per-lesson design counts rater differences as error, and it produced 0 and 0.51 at two lessons and 0 and 0.36 at one. The match of the 0.39 single-lesson mean to the literature's 0.39 is therefore not a like-for-like test, and the configuration ranking the abstract presents as a finding (same peer > same coach > different peer) is exactly the ordering that mechanical placement of rater variance predicts, a point the Discussion approaches but never names. The paper's prose also drifts from its exhibits more than a reader can tolerate without checking: Table 2's rows labeled "single observation" are two-lesson values; the Introduction swaps the clinical-practice relative and absolute ranges; the single-student survey range is 0.03 to 0.25 on p. 3 and 0.02 to 0.35 on p. 18; the Figure 1 narrative describes one-lesson levels as "rated twice"; Figure 2's clinical-practice panels cannot be regenerated from Table 3; and Table 1 and Table 3 disagree on a teacher count and on how 2014 surveys were administered. Add that the sample construction cannot be reconciled with the stated two-lesson, one-rater design (80 clinical-practice entries from a 32-teacher cohort in 2014), that the prior-study benchmark lives in an unavailable supplement with an inconsistent count (44 vs. 45), and that the promised data and code have no locator in the main text, and the right posture is: cite the paper as a transparent, well-hedged descriptive case of what practitioner-run measurement looks like in a middle-income nonprofit, quote every number from Tables 2 and 3 rather than the text, and treat the comparability claim and the rater-configuration contrasts as hypotheses the design cannot test.

> **Correction (2026-09-26).** Both counts are right. Supplemental Table A.1 lists 44 observation-based reliability estimates plus one student-survey estimate, 45 in all; pp. 3 and 15 count the observation estimates and p. 6 the whole table, as the Methods sub-review guessed. The supplement is now available: its mean of 0.391 over the 45 estimates matches the paper's pooled one-lesson mean, but by design it splits into 0.60 (same peer), 0.39 (same coach) and 0.18 (different peer), so the comparability point above stands. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the online supplement.

#### Key Strengths

- A genuinely new setting, honestly framed. Operational, formative-use observation and survey data from a middle-income country, collected by practitioners with a one-hour training, an in-house composite protocol with "no back-translation or piloting" (p. 11), and logistics-driven rater assignment (pp. 8-9). The authors call this a joint "stress test" (p. 9) and say plainly they cannot separate country, instrument, rater, and quality-assurance differences (p. 21).
- The estimation layer is fully regenerable. All 24 coefficients, 12 SEMs, and 12 teacher-effect SDs in Tables 2 and 3 reproduce to two decimals from the printed variance components with Eqs. 3-7 and 9-10; Figure 1 reproduces from Table 2; the text's single-lesson values (0.22, 0.36, 0.61, 0.60, 0, 0.36, 0.47, 0.50; mean 0.39) reproduce at n = 1. Few G-theory papers publish enough for readers to run their own D-studies.
- The D-study guidance is correct, practical, and costed. A third lesson adds 6 to 9 pp. of relative reliability in clinical practice and a third occasion adds 8 pp. in the school year, with 3 to 6 and 5 pp. thereafter (verified from Table 2); adding survey respondents from a class already surveyed is nearly free (p. 21); adding a school-year visit costs a coach trip (pp. 17-18).
- The Discussion is more careful than the abstract. It declines to read rater-type differences as properties of raters (p. 21), warns that D-study recommendations are imprecise (p. 22, citing Himmelsbach & Gilbert, 2025), notes that unmodeled facets may inflate coefficients (p. 22), and gives the most actionable advice in the paper: build limited randomization and double scoring into operations (p. 22).
- The variation across contexts and years is real enough to support the paper's narrower message. Practitioners should not import benchmarks from research settings; same-coach clinical-practice reliability moves from 0.34 to 0.52 across years, school-year survey reliability from 0.85 to 0.59, and one 25-teacher cell yields a teacher variance of zero.

#### Key Concerns

- Rater variance lands in a different place in each design, and the paper never says so. Peers scored only one teacher (p. 8), so in the same-peer design peer stringency and peer-by-teacher interaction are absorbed into the teacher component, inflating 0.75/0.71; in the per-coach studies the coach main effect is a constant and vanishes from both error terms; only the different-peer design counts rater variance as error (0 and 0.51). The 2014 same-peer and different-peer samples (25 and 25 from a 32-teacher cohort) must overlap by at least 18 teachers, yet the teacher variance is 0.210 in one and 0 in the other (Table 2, cols. 3 and 5), which is hard to explain by range restriction, the paper's leading candidate on p. 17. The abstract nonetheless presents reliability as depending on "rater assignment configurations."
- The comparability headline is not a like-for-like comparison. The 0.39 mean averages coefficients where rater variance is error, held fixed, and part of true score; the designs closest to research practice (raters rotating across lessons) average about 0.18. The literature benchmark itself (Table A.1) is in an unavailable supplement and is counted as 44 estimates on pp. 3 and 15 but 45 on p. 6. The literature review also finds the paper's descriptions of its two anchor designs wrong: Hill, Charalambous, and Kraft (2012) is said to have "only one observation per teacher" and Ho and Kane (2013) "an average of 46," which counts scores rather than lessons; and Praetorius et al. (2014), placed inside the CLASS score range, did not use CLASS.

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** Both counts are right. Supplemental Table A.1 lists 44 observation-based reliability estimates plus one student-survey estimate, 45 in all; pp. 3 and 15 count the observation estimates and p. 6 the whole table, as the Methods sub-review guessed. The supplement is now available: its mean of 0.391 over the 45 estimates matches the paper's pooled one-lesson mean, but by design it splits into 0.60 (same peer), 0.39 (same coach) and 0.18 (different peer), so the comparability point above stands. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the online supplement.

- The prose cannot substitute for the exhibits. Fifteen confirmed text-exhibit mismatches (consolidated in the writing review) include mislabeled "single observation" rows in Tables 2 and 3; the p. 3 swap of relative and absolute ranges; the p. 17 narrative describing one-lesson levels (0.2 to 0.6; 0.4 to 0.5) as "rated twice," citing "four lessons" for a one-lesson gain, and pointing to a panel that is flat at zero; the p. 18 single-rater range (0.02 to 0.35) that Table 3 does not support; Figure 2 panels A and B, which read roughly 0.24 and 0.69 near the operational respondent counts where Table 3 reports 0.33 and 0.58; "varied little" year to year when same-coach reliability moves 0.34 to 0.52; and "all but one" scenario improving when all four survey curves rise.
- Samples are small and their construction is undocumented. Columns rest on 20 to 48 teachers; the clinical-practice per-coach fits average four to five teachers each (30/7, 37/8); teacher variances sit at about one standard error in three columns (0.034 (0.028), 0.037 (0.030), 0.007 (0.006)); no SE or interval is given for any coefficient. Table 1's 80 (2014) and 100 (2015) clinical-practice entries cannot come from 32 and 45 teachers under "two lessons, one rater per lesson" (p. 8) without an unreported allocation rule; the exclusion rule ("observed fewer times than the rest," p. 9) has no threshold or counts; and whether per-coach components or coefficients were averaged, and how their SEs were formed, is unstated.
- Verification depends on materials that do not travel with the article. The paper says data and code are "available with this paper" (p. 22) but gives no repository, DOI, URL, software, or permission statement; Table A.1, the instrument descriptions, the correlations in Tables A.2-A.5, and the score distributions are all in an unavailable supplement.

#### What to Rely On

- The published variance components and the coefficients computed from them. Tables 2 and 3 are internally consistent and regenerable; the SDs, SEMs, and coefficients are exact functions of the components at the operational design (two lessons or occasions; the average class of about 19 to 26 students).
- The two-lesson, same-rater observation coefficients as descriptions of lesson-to-lesson consistency for a fixed rater: 0.34 to 0.75 relative and 0.29 to 0.71 absolute in clinical practice, 0.63 to 0.66 and 0.44 to 0.59 in the school year (Table 2). Describe them that way when citing.
- The different-peer-per-lesson coefficients (0 and 0.51 at two lessons; 0 and 0.36 at one) as the paper's only estimates in which rater differences count as error, and hence the most conservative and most research-comparable numbers in it.
- The full-class survey coefficients (relative 0.33 and 0.58 in clinical practice, 0.85 and 0.59 in the school year; Table 3) and the single-student values recomputed from them (0.03, 0.07, 0.25, 0.07), which match the Introduction's 0.03 to 0.25.
- The shape of the D-study returns: a third clinical-practice lesson adds 6 to 9 pp. relative and roughly 3 to 7 pp. absolute; a third school-year occasion adds 8 pp.; a fourth adds 3 to 6 and 5 pp.; adding five survey respondents to a class of ten adds about 7 to 10 pp. in clinical practice and 6 to 9 pp. relative in the school year (all verified from Tables 2 and 3).
- The paper's narrow recommendation: reliability under operational conditions is design-dependent and year-dependent, so practitioners should estimate it under their own design, and should build in double scoring and some randomization so that rater variance can be estimated (p. 22).
- The documentation of what practitioner-run measurement looked like in this program: a one-hour training with one practice rating (pp. 7-8), a composite of five U.S. protocols translated without back-translation or piloting (p. 11), a translated Tripod survey (p. 11), and formative use for allocating coaching (p. 7).

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- "Comparable to those from research in high-income countries" (abstract; pp. 3, 15) — the 0.39-vs-0.39 match averages designs with three different error definitions; in seven of eight observation analyses rater variance never enters the error term, and the one design where it does gives 0 and 0.51. The benchmark (Table A.1) is unavailable and inconsistently counted (44 vs. 45).

  > **Correction (2026-09-26).** Both counts are right. Supplemental Table A.1 lists 44 observation-based reliability estimates plus one student-survey estimate, 45 in all; pp. 3 and 15 count the observation estimates and p. 6 the whole table, as the Methods sub-review guessed. The supplement is now available: its mean of 0.391 over the 45 estimates matches the paper's pooled one-lesson mean, but by design it splits into 0.60 (same peer), 0.39 (same coach) and 0.18 (different peer), so the comparability point above stands. Found during the September 2026 reconciliation audit; confirmed against the online supplement.

- "Depends upon ... rater assignment configurations" and the same-peer > same-coach > different-peer ordering (abstract; pp. 15, 21) — assignment was non-random (pp. 8-9, 17), coaches were analyzed one at a time while peers were pooled, and the ordering is what mechanical placement of rater variance predicts. The authors themselves decline to read it as a property of rater types (p. 21); the abstract does not carry that qualifier.
- "From 0 to 0.75" as a substantive range — the 0 is a negative teacher-variance estimate truncated at zero in a 25-teacher cell (Table 2, col. 5) with no quantified uncertainty; the 0.75 comes from a design in which the rater's leniency toward the teacher counts as true score.
- Table 2's "Reliability of single observation" and "SEM of a single observation" rows, and the p. 15 confidence intervals built on them — these are two-lesson or two-occasion values (they reproduce only at n = 2). One-lesson relative coefficients are 0 to 0.61 (p. 15); one-lesson SEMs run about 0.26 to 0.48, not 0.18 to 0.34, and the intervals use the relative SEM to bracket an absolute score.
- Any survey number taken from Figure 2 or the Results narrative on pp. 18-20 — panels A and B do not regenerate from Table 3 (panel B is consistent with the rater:teacher and residual components being transposed, though this is not proven); the Results follow the figure while the Introduction follows the table. Use Table 3 and the p. 3 increments.
- The p. 18 single-rater survey range "0.02 to 0.35" — recomputation from Table 3 gives 0.03 to 0.25, as on p. 3.
- The Introduction's clinical-practice ranges "relative (absolute) error varied from 0 to 0.71 (0-0.75)" (p. 3) — swapped; Table 2 and p. 15 give relative 0 to 0.75 and absolute 0 to 0.71.
- The claim that the 2015 survey drop (0.85 to 0.59) reflects switching to different classes across occasions (abstract; p. 19) — each occasion is analyzed separately, so the switch cannot mechanically enter a single occasion's coefficient; the drop comes from teacher variance (0.094 to 0.020), and clinical-practice surveys vary as much (0.33 to 0.58) with no design change. The abstract's "coinciding with" is appropriately noncausal; do not upgrade it.
- The qualitative characterizations "varied little from one year to the next" (p. 17), clinical-practice surveys "more variable" than school-year surveys (p. 19), and raters helping "in all but one" scenario (p. 19) — each is contradicted by Tables 2-3 or Figure 2.
- Per-coach coefficients as organization-wide reliability — they hold coach stringency fixed, so they describe comparisons among teachers who share a coach; if ExA allocates support across coaches, reliability for that decision is lower than reported and unestimated.
- The paper's descriptions of prior designs (Hill et al., 2012 "one observation per teacher"; Ho & Kane, 2013 "average of 46"; Praetorius et al., 2014 inside the CLASS range; Schweig's 0.16 as a "single Tripod administration" set against single-student values) — check the originals before repeating; several reference-list years are also wrong (Jackson is JPE 2018; Dee & Wyckoff JPAM 2015; Kimball et al. and Milanowski PJE 2004; Patrick et al. AERJ 2020; RESET has no reference entry).
- "One of the first" G-studies in an LMIC and "no empirical examinations" (p. 21) — reliability evidence for research-administered LMIC observation tools exists (e.g., Molina et al., 2020 on Teach in Pakistan, co-authored by Ho); the defensible novelty is practitioner-administered, formative-use data.
- Generalization to the Teach for All network and to public evaluation systems — one organization, one province, roughly 100 alternative-pathway novices, data from 2014-2015, a bespoke protocol, and coach and novice-peer raters.

### Methods Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

This is a small, carefully hedged G-theory study of real-world data, and the core arithmetic holds up. I reproduced every generalizability coefficient and SEM in Tables 2 and 3 from the reported variance components using Eqs. 3–10. The paper's most quotable comparisons are shakier. Its designs differ in where rater effects land: the rater is error in one design, held fixed in another, and counted as true score in a third. That makes the ranking of rater configurations, and the "remarkably close" match to the literature's single-observation mean of 0.39, partly an artifact of what each design counts as error. Several text–table and figure–table mismatches in the D-study narrative mean readers should work from the tables rather than the prose.

**Strengths:**

- **The calculations check out.** Using the paper's own equations, the relative and absolute coefficients, SDs of the teacher effect, and SEMs in Table 2 (all eight columns, p. 16) and Table 3 (all four columns, p. 19) reproduce to the reported precision. Example: Table 2, col. 1 gives δ = 0.086/2 + 0.059/6 + 0.142/12 = 0.0647, so Eρ² = 0.034/(0.034 + 0.0647) = 0.34, Φ = 0.29, and SEM = 0.254. The single-observation relative coefficients the text reports (range 0–0.61, mean 0.39; p. 15) also reproduce when n_l = n_o = 1 and n_d = 6.
- **Figure 1 matches Table 2.** The D-study curves in Figure 1 (p. 18) agree with my recomputation from Table 2, e.g., panel G: 0.47, 0.63, 0.71, and 0.85 at 1, 2, 3, and 8 occasions.
- **The designs are described honestly.** The paper names the design notation for each analysis (Table 1, col. 7, p. 10), states which facets cannot be estimated (rater stringency in the observation designs, pp. 8–9; lesson or occasion in the survey designs, pp. 8–9), and admits that raters were not randomly assigned (pp. 8–9, 17).
- **The hedging is appropriate.** The authors report standard errors for the variance components and warn against Wald intervals near the boundary (p. 12). They flag range restriction and nonrandom pairing (p. 17), acknowledge that unmodeled facets may inflate reliability (p. 22), and read rater-type differences as evidence that reliability is "sensitive to design features" rather than as a property of rater types (p. 21).
- **It uses real operational data.** Two years, two contexts, and several rater configurations of practitioner-collected data are rare in this literature. The descriptive contribution does not depend on any causal design.

**Weaknesses:**

- **Rater effects land in different places in each design, which drives the configuration ranking.**
  - In the **same-peer** designs, each peer scores only one teacher (coaches, "but not peers," scored multiple teachers; p. 8). Peer stringency and the peer-by-teacher interaction are therefore absorbed into the *teacher* (universe-score) variance, which inflates Eρ² and Φ.
  - In the **different-peer** designs, peer effects fall into Lesson:Teacher, i.e., into error.
  - In the **per-coach** studies, the coach main effect is constant within each study and drops out of both δ and Δ. Coach-by-teacher interaction sits in the teacher variance.
  - As a result, the same-peer coefficients (0.75/0.71), the same-coach coefficients (0.34–0.52), and the different-peer coefficients (0–0.51) (Table 2, p. 16) answer different generalizability questions.
- **Internal evidence that this is mechanical.** In 2014, the entering cohort had 32 teachers (p. 9), yet the same-peer and different-peer clinical-practice analyses each include 25 (Table 1, p. 10). At least 18 teachers must therefore appear in both. Those largely overlapping teachers yield teacher variance of 0.210 under same-peer scoring and 0 under different-peer scoring (Table 2, cols. 3 and 5). This is my inference from reported counts. It fits confounding of peer effects with the teacher component better than it fits a population difference.
- **The literature comparison is not like-for-like.** The single-observation mean of 0.39 (p. 15; also p. 3) averages coefficients where rater variance is error (different-peer: 0 and 0.36 by my recomputation), held fixed (per-coach: 0.22, 0.36, 0.47, 0.50), and part of true score (same-peer: 0.61, 0.60). The match to the literature's 0.39 (Table A.1, unavailable to me) is therefore not evidence that practitioner-collected data are as reliable as research data.
- **The per-coach clinical-practice studies are extremely small.** They cover 30 teachers across 7 coaches (2014) and 37 across 8 (2015), roughly 4–5 teachers per coach-specific REML fit (Table 1, p. 10). The paper does not say how component SEs were combined across coaches, and averaging components that were truncated at zero biases the averages upward. No SEs or intervals are given for any generalizability coefficient or D-study point, even though these are the headline quantities.
- **Table rows are mislabeled (checkable).** Table 2's rows "SEM of a single observation" and "Reliability of single observation" (p. 16) reproduce only at the *two*-lesson or two-occasion design, not at n = 1. For example, col. 1 gives 0.34 at n_l = 2 and 0.22 at n_l = 1. Likewise, Table 3's "single observation" rows reproduce at the average class size of 18.5–25.5 respondents, not at a single student. The confidence intervals on p. 15 ([2.65, 3.35] and [2.33, 3.67]) therefore describe two-lesson averages. They also use the relative-error SEM to bracket a score's absolute location, where √Δ would be the right quantity. At n_l = 1, the SEM is 0.35 (col. 1) and 0.48 (col. 5), not 0.184–0.340.
- **Text–table mismatches in the D-study narrative (p. 17).**
  - The text says relative reliability in clinical practice "is between 0.2 and 0.6 when each teacher is rated twice." The two-lesson values in Table 2 are 0.34–0.75 excluding 2014 different-peer. The 0.2–0.6 range matches the *one*-lesson values (0.22–0.61).
  - Likewise, "between 0.4 and 0.5 when each teacher is rated twice" for the school year contradicts Table 2's 0.63 and 0.66, but matches my one-occasion values (0.47, 0.50).
  - The claimed absolute range "between 0.3 and 0.7" for panels A–B and E–F does not match Table 2 (0.29, 0.33, 0, 0.48).
- **Figure 2 panels A–B do not match Table 3.** At 10 students, Eq. 12 applied to Table 3 gives clinical-practice relative coefficients of 0.21 (2014) and 0.43 (2015). Figure 2 and the text show about 0.15 and 0.55 (p. 20). At 18.5 respondents, panel B shows about 0.68, while Table 3, col. 2 reports 0.58 for that design. Panel D does match Table 3. The introduction's survey D-study gains ("7 to 10 pp.," "6 to 9 pp.," and "4 pp.," p. 3) agree with my Table-3-based recomputation. The Results text (p. 20) instead follows the figure. At least one of the table and figure appears stale.
- **Other checkable inconsistencies.**
  - The introduction swaps the clinical-practice ranges: "relative (absolute) error varied from 0 to 0.71 (0–0.75)" (p. 3), whereas Table 2 gives relative 0–0.75 and absolute 0–0.71.
  - Single-student survey coefficients are given as "0.03 to 0.25" on p. 3 but "0.02 to 0.35" on p. 18. My recomputation from Table 3 gives 0.03–0.25.
  - The 2015 school-year survey sample is 28 teachers in Table 1 (p. 10) but 25 in Table 3 (p. 19).
  - Table 1 labels 2014 school-year surveys "All different students per occasion," but p. 9 says ExA surveyed the same group of students on both occasions in 2014.
  - The literature count is "45 reliability estimates" on p. 6 but "44 estimates" on pp. 3 and 15. This may reconcile if one of the 45 is the survey estimate; I cannot check without Table A.1.
- **Sample construction is underdescribed.** Page 8 says each clinical-practice teacher "was observed on two lessons, with one rater scoring each lesson." Yet the 2014 clinical-practice analyses contain 30 + 25 + 25 = 80 teacher entries from a 32-teacher cohort, and 2015 contains 100 entries from 45 (Table 1; p. 9). Most teachers must therefore have been observed on more than two lessons. The paper does not explain how lessons were allocated to configurations, or which teachers were dropped for having "fewer" observations (p. 9).
- **The random-facet assumptions shape the D-study.**
  - The school-year occasion facet has only two levels, mid-year and end-of-year (p. 8). Its main effect in 2015 (0.084, SE 0.095; Table 2, col. 8) makes up about 45% of that column's absolute error variance by my calculation, and it is arguably a systematic time trend rather than a random draw.
  - Teacher-by-occasion variance can include real within-year change, which D-studies then treat as error.
  - Domains are treated as random (p. 12), which is conservative for the composite, but ExA uses *domain-level* scores for decisions (p. 12). Domain-level reliability is not reported and would be lower.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Take away the qualitative findings.** Practitioner-collected observations and surveys can reach moderate reliability in the current design, and a third lesson or occasion or five more students yields single-digit percentage-point gains with diminishing returns. The D-study increments for observations (roughly 6–9 pp. for a third lesson, about 8 pp. for a third occasion; p. 3) reproduce from Table 2.
- **Do not read the configuration ranking as a finding about raters.** Same peer > same coach > different peer (Table 2) mostly reflects where rater variance sits in each design. Only the different-peer design counts rater differences as error, so it is the closest analogue to research G-studies that rotate raters. Its values (0 and 0.51 at two lessons; 0 and 0.36 for a single lesson) are the most conservative numbers in the paper.
- **Do not treat the "remarkably close" 0.39 match to the literature as evidence** that practitioner-led reliability equals research-setting reliability. It averages over designs with different error definitions.
- **The per-coach coefficients assume teachers are only compared with others who have the same coach.** If ExA compares teachers across coaches when allocating support, coach stringency adds error the paper did not estimate, and reliability for those decisions would be lower than reported.
- **Treat Table 2's "single observation" rows as two-lesson or two-occasion values**, and Table 3's as full-class values. For the reliability of one lesson or one student, use the text's recomputed figures (p. 15; p. 3 for surveys) or recompute them from the components.
- **When the D-study text and the tables disagree, trust the tables.** For surveys, the introduction's numbers (p. 3) are consistent with Table 3; the Results narrative and Figure 2 A–B are not.
- **Treat the zero reliability for 2014 different-peer observations** (teacher variance 0 with SE 0, Table 2, col. 5) as a boundary estimate from 25 teachers, not as proof of pure noise. Its uncertainty is not quantified.
- **Do not read the 2015 school-year survey drop (0.85 to 0.59) as a design effect.** Each occasion is analyzed separately (p. 9), so switching to different classes across occasions cannot mechanically change a single occasion's coefficient. The drop coincides with lower teacher variance (0.094 vs. 0.020, Table 3). The abstract's "coinciding with" wording is appropriately noncausal.
- **Verify against the promised data and code before reusing these numbers.** The Supplemental Appendices (Table A.1, Tables A.2–A.5, Figures A.1–A.4, instrument details) and the replication files were not available for this review.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*What the design can and cannot identify.* Every G-study here has one rater per lesson, occasion, or class, so no design separates rater variance from other facets directly. The key interpretive question is what each design's teacher component contains.

- **Clinical-practice d×(l:t) with the same peer on both lessons.** The peer is effectively nested in the teacher (peers did not observe multiple teachers, p. 8). The peer main effect and the peer-by-teacher interaction are therefore indistinguishable from true teacher differences and are counted as universe-score variance. The estimand is "the teacher as seen by that teacher's particular peer." That is internally consistent, but it is not reliability generalizing over raters.
- **Different peer per lesson.** Peer effects are confounded with Lesson:Teacher and counted as error. This is the only design where rater stringency penalizes reliability.
- **Per-coach studies, in clinical practice and in the school year.** Within a study the coach is a fixed constant. The coach main effect vanishes from both relative and absolute error, and coach-by-teacher interaction joins the teacher component. The estimand is reliability for comparing teachers who share a coach.

The paper describes the designs correctly in G-theory notation but never spells out these consequences. The discussion's explanation that "agreement among new teachers is likely rarer than consistency in the ratings of a teacher across lessons" (p. 21) comes close, and the authors decline to attribute differences to rater types. Even so, the introduction and abstract present the level and spread of reliability "across rater assignment configurations" as a finding, and the pooled means (0.48 relative in clinical practice, p. 15) average across estimands. My arithmetic check confirms 0.48 = mean(0.34, 0.52, 0.75, 0.75, 0, 0.51) and 0.42 for absolute (Table 2, p. 16).

The overlap argument makes the point concrete. Clinical practice covers only the 2014 and 2015 entering cohorts (32 and 45 teachers, p. 9). The same-peer and different-peer samples (25 and 25 in 2014; 43 and 20 in 2015, Table 1) must share at least 18 teachers in each year. For essentially the same 2014 teachers, estimated teacher variance swings from 0.210 to 0. It is hard to explain that by range restriction, the paper's leading candidate on p. 17. It is what one expects when peer stringency is counted as true score in one design and as error in the other.

A pooled model with teachers nested in coaches could have estimated between-coach variance directly, but none is reported. That quantity matters for ExA's actual use, allocating support across the whole cohort. The practical implication is that the per-coach coefficients (0.34–0.66, Table 2, cols. 1–2 and 7–8) are upper bounds for organization-wide comparisons.

*Estimation with tiny samples.* The clinical-practice per-coach fits average about 4–5 teachers each (30/7 and 37/8; Table 1). Each fit estimates five variance components, and the teacher variance rests on a handful of teachers. REML with boundary truncation at this scale is noisy and biased upward once truncated components are averaged. The paper reports delta-method SEs for averaged components (e.g., teacher variance 0.034 with SE 0.028, Table 2, col. 1) but does not say how per-coach SEs were combined. It reports no uncertainty for the coefficients themselves.

The recomputed coefficients equal those implied by the averaged components, which suggests coefficients were computed from averaged components rather than averaged across coaches. Table 1's note says "report the average results," which is ambiguous. For school-year surveys, Figure 2 panel C sits slightly above my Table-3-based curve (e.g., absolute about 0.67 vs. 0.62 at 10 students), which would be consistent with the other averaging order. Only the code can settle this.

The authors' caution in the Discussion is well placed, including the citation to Himmelsbach and Gilbert (2025) on Bayesian D-studies (p. 22). With coefficients this imprecise, differences such as 0.34 vs. 0.52 (same coach, 2014 vs. 2015) should not be read as real.

*Labeling and narrative accuracy.* The equations are standard and correctly implemented. The one exception is on paper: Eqs. 11–12 (p. 14) leave n_l and n_r unprimed in the first term, a typo, since Figure 1 reproduces only with the primed version. The reporting layer has more slippage than the estimation layer.

- **Table 2 "single observation" rows.** They reproduce at n_l = 2 or n_o = 2 (e.g., SEM 0.254 = √0.0647 for col. 1). The worked confidence intervals on p. 15 therefore understate single-lesson uncertainty. The one-lesson SEM for 2014 different-peer is 0.48, not 0.34. Those intervals also use the relative SEM around an absolute score. For school year 2015, √Δ = 0.307 versus the reported 0.193, a sizable difference driven by the two-level occasion main effect.
- **The p. 17 narrative.** It describes one-lesson and one-occasion values as "rated twice." It also cites a panel (E) whose line is flat at zero as evidence of a 4–7 pp. gain.
- **Figure 2 panels A–B.** They cannot be reproduced from Table 3 via Eq. 12, and the Results text follows the figure. The introduction's survey D-study gains follow the table.

None of these errors changes the qualitative conclusions, but a reader quoting specific numbers could quote the wrong one.

*Surveys.* The d×(r:t) design treats students as interchangeable raters nested in teachers, and each teacher is rated by a single class per occasion. Class composition and peer climate are therefore confounded with the teacher component, a point the authors partly acknowledge (p. 8, citing Seidel, 2006). The D-study "add five students from the same class" is valid within that universe, but it says nothing about generalizing across classes.

Clinical-practice students were volunteers, and scores are near the ceiling (means 4.47 and 4.44 on a 1–5 scale, Table 1). That likely explains the tiny 2014 teacher variance (0.007, Table 3). The survey coefficients use the "average number of raters." For unbalanced nested designs a harmonic mean is the usual choice, and an arithmetic mean slightly overstates reliability, though the effect is minor here.

*Generalizability of the headline.* The paper frames itself as a joint "stress test" of whether research-setting reliability transports to practitioner settings (p. 9). It candidly notes that country, instrument, raters, and quality assurance all differ at once (p. 21). The design supports "reliability varies a lot across operational configurations and years, so estimate your own." That is the paper's main recommendation (p. 22), and it is well supported, partly *because* the configurations define error differently. The design does not support "practitioner reliability is comparable to research reliability." The data behind the paper's comparative statements are thinner than they appear: 8 observation coefficients, several from 4–5-teacher per-coach fits, and 4 survey coefficients, set against a literature summary (Table A.1) I could not inspect.

*What I could not assess.* Supplemental Appendices A and B (Table A.1, Tables A.2–A.5, Figures A.1–A.4, instrument descriptions) and the promised data and code were unavailable. I therefore could not verify:

- the literature benchmarks (0.39 mean, 0.38 median, 44 or 45 estimates);
- whether per-coach coefficients or components were averaged;
- how lessons were allocated to configurations;
- the REML and SE implementation.

My checks cover every coefficient in Tables 2–3, the D-study curves in Figures 1–2 (read visually), and the text's numerical claims on pp. 3, 15, 17–20.

---

### Literature Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper places itself correctly within the U.S. canon of G-studies on classroom observation (MET, Hill/Charalambous/Kraft 2012, Ho & Kane 2013, Meyer et al. 2011, Praetorius et al. 2014, van der Lans et al. 2016). It is also frank that its comparison to that canon is a joint "stress test" rather than a clean contrast. But its central benchmark, a mean single-observation reliability of 0.39 across "44" or "45" prior estimates, cannot be checked from the main text. Several descriptions of prior studies are wrong or look doubtful. The claims that practitioner-collected data and LMIC reliability evidence are new are overstated. The student-survey comparison rests on one prior estimate, yet a large multilevel literature on student-rating reliability exists and goes unused.

**Strengths:**

- *(Checkable)* The Prior Research section (pp. 4–6) explains the step from classical test theory to G-theory clearly and cites the standard sources (Cronbach et al., 1972; Brennan, 2001; Shavelson & Webb, 1991). It also names the specific quality-assurance tools used in research settings (rater certification, master coding, validation engines; p. 6, citing Jerald, 2012; McClellan, 2013; MET Project, 2010; Joe et al., 2013). This gives readers a concrete list of what practitioner settings usually lack.
- *(Checkable)* The paper summarizes the prior G-study base in numbers rather than impressions. It gives the instrument mix, sample sizes (median 48 teachers; 73% under 100), mean and SD/SEM patterns, and the share of single-observation estimates at or above 0.70 (pp. 5–6, citing Supplemental Table A.1). This is more systematic than most positioning sections in this literature.
- *(Checkable / interpretive)* The authors are candid about confounding. They call the study a joint test of country, instrument, rater, and quality-assurance differences, and they disclaim separating these (p. 9, Measures; p. 21, Discussion). They state that reliability does not establish validity, citing the AERA/APA/NCME *Standards* (p. 9).
- *(Checkable)* Uncertainty in D-study projections is flagged (p. 22), as is the risk that unmodeled facets inflate coefficients (p. 22, citing Bell et al., 2012). Both points connect to the measurement literature in the right way.
- *(Interpretive)* Anchoring the study in Teach For All (p. 2, p. 7) is a sensible choice about who the audience is. Readers who run non-profit or ministry feedback systems will find the setting more relevant than MET districts.

**Weaknesses:**

- *(Checkable, main-text-only)* **The count of prior estimates is inconsistent.** The paper says the 0.39 mean and 0.38 median come from "44 estimates" (p. 3, Introduction; p. 15, Results), but the Prior Research section reports the same mean and median "across the 45 reliability estimates in Table A.1" (p. 6). The p. 6 shares are arithmetically consistent with a denominator of 45: 76% below 0.50 (34/45 = 75.6%) and 7% at or above 0.70 (3/45). One possible reconciliation is that 44 is observations only, with Schweig's (2014) single survey estimate excluded. The paper never says so, and I could not check it because Supplemental Appendix A (Table A.1) was not available to me.

  *See the correction note in the synthesis: both counts are right.*

- *(Checkable against the cited source)* **Hill, Charalambous, & Kraft (2012) is mischaracterized.** The paper lists this study as an extreme case "with only one observation per teacher" (pp. 5–6). I checked the article itself. Its G-study used 8 teachers with three lessons each, and every lesson was scored by nine certified raters in a lessons-nested-in-teachers, crossed-with-raters design. In the same sentence, Ho & Kane (2013) is said to have "an average of 46" observations per teacher (p. 6). The MET report shows that figure counts *scores* per teacher (67 teachers, four lessons each, 129 raters). So the paper counts "observations" in two different ways for its two anchor cases, and its summary of the range of designs cannot be relied on as stated.
- *(Checkable / partly from memory)* **Praetorius et al. (2014) is placed in the CLASS range.** The paper cites Praetorius et al.'s "Cognitive Activation domain at 1.93" as the low end of CLASS Instructional Support means and as a possible floor effect on a 1–7 scale (p. 6). Praetorius et al. did not use CLASS. They used high-inference ratings of the German "three basic dimensions." From memory, and unverified, that scale was 1–4, and on a 1–4 scale 1.93 is not near the floor. The paper also does not report that study's headline finding, which I confirmed from its abstract: one lesson was enough for classroom management and personal learning support, while cognitive activation needed about nine lessons. That finding complicates the paper's blanket conclusion that a single observation is "generally insufficient ... regardless of the instrument used" (p. 6).
- *(Checkable)* **The single-rater survey figures conflict between sections.** The Introduction gives a range of "0.03 to 0.25" (p. 3). The Results give "0.02 to 0.35" (p. 18). My recomputation from the Table 3 variance components (p. 19; n_r = 1, n_d = 7) gives about 0.03, 0.07, 0.25, and 0.07, which supports p. 3. The Results also describe the comparison figure as "Schweig's (2014) estimate of 0.16 for a single Tripod administration" (pp. 18–19). A "single administration" normally means a whole class of respondents, not one student. If 0.16 is a per-administration figure, it should be compared with the paper's full-administration coefficients (0.33–0.85, Table 3), not with its single-student ones. From Schweig's abstract, the article compares approaches to aggregation error in school- and classroom-environment surveys. I could not confirm that it used Tripod or what unit 0.16 refers to.
- *(Interpretive, grounded in checkable numbers)* **The "remarkably close" comparison (pp. 3, 15) pools estimates that are not like-for-like.** In the paper's own designs where the same rater scores both lessons, rater stringency, and in the peer designs rater × teacher interaction, is absorbed into the "teacher" component. Prior single-observation estimates that treat raters as random count that variance as error. My recomputation of the paper's single-observation coefficients from Table 2 (p. 16) gives about 0.22, 0.36, 0.61, and 0.60 for the same-coach and same-peer clinical designs, 0 and 0.36 for the different-peer designs, and 0.47 and 0.50 for the school year. These average to the reported 0.39. The only designs in which raters vary across lessons, as in most of the research base, average about 0.18. The match on means may therefore be partly an artifact of design. Ho & Kane (2013), co-authored by one of these authors, found that first impressions carry over when the same rater sees several lessons. That is the mechanism most likely to inflate the same-peer coefficients (0.75), but the paper does not bring it in.
- *(Checkable)* **Table 2's row labels invite misreading against the literature.** The rows labeled "Reliability of single observation" and "SEM of a single observation" (p. 16) actually report two-lesson coefficients. For example, column 1's 0.34 and 0.254 reproduce exactly with n_l = 2 and n_d = 6. The single-lesson values are the ones in the text (0 to 0.61, p. 15). A reader who sets Table 2 against Table A.1 or against MET single-observation figures would see this sample as far more reliable than it is. The p. 15 illustration of confidence intervals has the same problem, since it uses these SEMs "for a single observation."
- *(Own knowledge, partly verified)* **The novelty claims are stronger than the literature supports.** The Discussion says "there have been no empirical examinations of this question" in LMICs (p. 21), and the abstract says "one of the first" G-studies. Some reliability evidence does exist for observation tools used in LMICs. Molina et al. (2020, *Teaching and Teacher Education*), co-authored by Ho, report inter-rater reliability and validity for the World Bank's Teach tool in Punjab, Pakistan, with observers trained locally. The paper cites only the 2018 World Bank report version (Molina et al., 2018) and only as an example of adapted instruments (pp. 9, 21). OECD's Global Teaching InSights video study (2020), from memory, documents rater reliability in Chile, Colombia, and Mexico. Araujo et al. (2016, cited) report CLASS measurement properties in Ecuador. Most of these are research-administered, so the narrower claim, practitioner-administered in an LMIC, may still hold. The broader wording does not.
- *(Checkable / own knowledge)* **The contrast between research and practitioner settings is drawn too sharply.** The Introduction presents prior guidance as coming "largely from studies in which [measures] were administered for research purposes," with Glazerman et al. (2011) and Whitehurst et al. (2014) as the only exceptions (pp. 1–2). The Discussion says flatly that "prior G-studies relied on data collected for research" (p. 21). But Ho & Kane (2013) is titled *The Reliability of Classroom Observations by School Personnel*: its raters were Hillsborough principals and peer teachers, although they scored videos inside a research design. Its findings bear directly on this paper's coach-vs-peer contrast. Administrators spread their scores 50% more than peers did, rated their own teachers 0.1 points higher than other administrators did, and carried first impressions forward (MET report, pp. 4–5). None of this is used. Hill et al. (2012) likewise note that a district that has to use principals could not screen out raters who fail certification. That is the paper's core argument, but the paper does not credit it.
- *(Own knowledge)* **The student-survey literature is barely covered.** The paper treats one estimate as "the only estimate ... from prior research" (p. 3) and "the sole student survey estimate" (p. 6). That is true only inside a narrow search limited to formal G-studies. Educational psychology has a large literature on the reliability of aggregated student ratings (ICC(1)/ICC(2) in multilevel models) that answers the same question. Examples include Lüdtke et al. (2009, *Contemporary Educational Psychology*), Marsh et al. (2012, *Educational Psychologist*), Wagner et al. (2013, *Learning and Instruction*), and work on the Dutch/ICALT student-perception instruments by van der Lans, Maulana, and colleagues, including cross-national studies with Indonesia, South Africa, and Turkey. On Tripod specifically there is MET's student-survey reporting (Kane & Staiger, 2012, cited only for observations) and structural critiques (Wallace, Kelcey, & Ruzek, 2016, *AERJ*; Kuhfeld, 2017, *Educational Assessment*). All of these citations are from memory. The paper's single-student coefficients (about 0.03–0.25) fall in the range usually reported for single-student ICCs in that literature, so the omission weakens the paper's context more than its conclusions.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Do not repeat the "0.39 vs. 0.39" benchmark as evidence that practitioner reliability matches research reliability** without two caveats. First, the prior-estimate count (44 vs. 45) and the composition of Table A.1 cannot be checked from the article. Second, the paper's mean pools designs where the same rater scores both lessons with prior estimates that treat raters as random. The designs closest to the research standard (a different peer per lesson) average about 0.18 by my recomputation from Table 2.
- **Check the descriptions of prior studies before citing them from this paper.** Specifically: Hill, Charalambous, & Kraft (2012) had three lessons per teacher, not one. Ho & Kane's (2013) "46" is ratings per teacher, not lessons. Praetorius et al. (2014) is not a CLASS study and found one lesson sufficient for two of three dimensions. Schweig's (2014) 0.16 needs its unit of analysis confirmed.
- **Read Table 2 with care.** Rows labeled "single observation" report two-lesson reliabilities. Use the p. 15 text (0 to 0.61) for single-observation comparisons.
- **For the claim that practitioner ratings differ from research ratings, read these alongside the paper:** Ho & Kane (2013), on administrator vs. peer raters and carryover effects. Whitehurst, Chingos, & Lindquist (2014, cited) and Steinberg & Garrett (2016, *EEPA*), on how district observation scores depend on classroom composition. Chaplin et al. (2014, REL Mid-Atlantic), who use Pittsburgh's operational RISE/FfT and Tripod data. I checked that they report only internal consistency and note that multi-rater reliability could not be estimated from single-principal ratings, which is itself telling. Grissom & Loeb (2017, *EFP*) and Kraft & Gilmour (2017, cited), on leniency in practitioner ratings. Bell, Dobbelaer, Klette, & Visscher (2019, *School Effectiveness and School Improvement*), for a framework that treats reliability as a property of the whole observation *system*, which is essentially this paper's conclusion (own knowledge).
- **For the clinical-practice setting, read Bartanen & Kwok (2021, *AERJ* 58(5)).** I verified its abstract. It analyzes practitioner-collected observation scores during clinical teaching in a large Texas program and finds that differences in field supervisors' rating standards drive much of the variation, more than differences between preservice teachers do. This is the closest U.S. comparison to the paper's clinical-practice findings, and it points the same way as the paper's weak different-peer results. Gitomer et al. (2021, *AERJ*) on edTPA reliability is relevant for pre-service performance assessment (own knowledge).
- **For LMIC context, pair the paper with** Molina et al. (2020, *TATE*; Teach in Pakistan), OECD's *Global Teaching InSights* (2020) technical reporting on rater reliability in Chile, Colombia, and Mexico, and Bruns, Costa, & Cunha (2018, cited) and Bruns & Luque (2014, cited) on large-scale Stallings observation in Latin America (own knowledge, except Molina et al., whose abstract I verified). Cite this paper for *practitioner-administered, low-stakes, non-profit* reliability in a middle-income country. Do not cite it as the first reliability evidence on classroom observation in LMICs.
- **Reference-list errors** *(own knowledge, moderately confident)*. These are worth correcting before copying citations: Jackson's "What do test scores miss?" is *JPE* 2018, not 2020. Dee & Wyckoff's IMPACT article in *JPAM* 34 is 2015, not 2013. Kimball et al. and Milanowski in *Peabody Journal of Education* 79(4) are 2004, not 2009. Hafen et al. (35(5–6)) is 2015. Patrick et al. (*AERJ* 57(5)) is 2020. The RESET instrument is discussed on p. 6 but has no citation in the main reference list.

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Coverage and structure.* The Prior Research section (pp. 4–6) moves from value-added critiques (Rothstein, 2010; Papay, 2011; Jackson, 2018/"2020"; Kraft, 2019) to the multiple-measures argument (Kane & Staiger, 2012; Kane et al., 2014) and then to G-theory. For a measurement paper in EEPA this is a reasonable arc, and the economics-of-education citations are current and fairly described *(interpretive)*. The substance of the positioning, though, sits almost entirely in Supplemental Table A.1: 15 G-studies, 13 U.S. and 2 European, of which CLASS appears in seven, FfT in five, and MQI in three (p. 5). In the main text only a handful of these studies are named (Praetorius et al., 2014; van der Lans et al., 2016; Hill et al., 2012; Kane & Staiger, 2012; Ho & Kane, 2013; Mantzicopoulos et al., 2018; Patrick et al., 2020; Schweig, 2014). A reader of the published article alone cannot tell how the 15 were chosen (search strategy, inclusion rules) or how "estimates" were counted. **I did not have access to Supplemental Appendices A or B**, so I cannot say whether the appendix answers these questions. Readers should look at Table A.1 before relying on the benchmark.

Some well-known G-study and rater-effects work is missing from the main-text reference list. I cannot say whether it is in Table A.1. From memory: Mashburn, Meyer, Allen, & Pianta (2014, *EPM*) on observation length and order; Casabianca, Lockwood, & McCaffrey (2015, *EPM*) on rater drift over time; Cash, Hamre, Pianta, & Myers (2012, *ECRQ*) on rater calibration at scale; Bell et al. (2014) on observer cognition; and White (2018, *Educational Researcher*) on rater performance standards. The rater-drift and calibration papers matter here because the paper's explanation for lower clinical-practice reliability is that raters are "still getting used to" the protocol (p. 21). That explanation is exactly what the drift and calibration literature has studied *(interpretive)*.

*Accuracy of characterizations.* I checked three of the paper's descriptions against the original sources. Two were wrong in ways that matter. Hill et al. (2012) had three lessons per teacher, not one. Ho & Kane's (2013) "46" counts ratings, not lessons. So the claim that prior designs "typically" use three to eight observations per teacher (p. 5) mixes lessons and ratings, and readers should not reuse it. The third, the Praetorius et al. (2014) cognitive-activation mean, is placed among CLASS domains, and the article's main finding is left out. That finding matters because it is the clearest evidence in the canon that the number of lessons needed depends on the dimension. It supports the paper's own advice that practitioners should estimate reliability locally, but it undercuts the p. 6 generalization that one observation is insufficient "regardless of the instrument." A smaller point: all three single-observation estimates at or above 0.70 in the prior base come from kindergarten studies by one research group (Mantzicopoulos et al., 2018; Patrick et al., 2020; p. 6). Readers should take that clustering into account when judging how representative the upper tail is *(interpretive)*.

The paper describes G-theory as "increasingly used in teacher feedback systems in the United States" and supports this with Bell et al. (2012), Hill et al. (2012), Ho & Kane (2013), Kane & Staiger (2012), and Meyer et al. (2011) (p. 2). These are research studies, not descriptions of operational feedback systems. The claim about operational use may well be true, but these citations do not establish it *(checkable against the reference list; interpretive as to adequacy)*.

*Novelty claims.* The paper lists four ways it differs from prior work (p. 2). (1) Practitioner collection in a middle-income country: largely new for *practitioner-administered, operational* data, but the p. 21 claim of "no empirical examinations" ignores research-administered reliability work in LMICs, including a paper co-authored by Ho (Molina et al., 2020). (2) Instruments "adapted from widely used protocols," which the paper says reduces concerns about instrument construction: this sits awkwardly with the paper's own account that the observation protocol is a new composite of five instruments, translated without back-translation or piloting (p. 11), and with the Discussion's admission that the instruments differ from prior work (p. 21). The survey, a translation of Tripod, is a much cleaner comparison than the observation protocol. (3) Variation across years, settings, and rater configurations: new relative to most single-administration G-studies, and the most useful contribution *(interpretive)*. (4) Relevance to the Teach For All network: plausible but untested. I would add one thing the paper undersells. Treating G-theory as a routine tool for practitioners, including the advice to build limited double-scoring into operations (p. 22), is a useful bridge to organizations that rarely see this literature. Readers should cite the paper for that framing and for the operational variability it documents, not for a clean comparison between research and practice.

*Engagement with conflicting evidence.* The paper's discussion of how to read the rater-assignment differences (p. 21) lists range restriction, pairing, and coaches inflating scores. It does not list the one mechanism the measurement literature points to first: in same-rater designs, rater effects are counted as teacher variance. Ho & Kane (2013) show that first impressions carry over and that different kinds of raters produce different score spreads. MET's own guidance, quoted on p. 5, recommends lessons "each with a different rater" for exactly this reason. Once that is taken into account, the evidence in this paper's own tables, and in Bartanen & Kwok's (2021) clinical-teaching data, suggests that practitioner-assigned ratings which separate raters from teachers are *less* reliable than the research base. That is not the "comparable" conclusion in the abstract. The paper partly concedes this on p. 22 (omitted facets may lead it to "overestimate the reliability"), but it does not carry the concession back to the benchmark comparison *(interpretive)*.

On surveys, the paper's single-student coefficients are close to the student-rating ICCs usually reported in the multilevel literature, from memory. Its full-administration coefficients (0.33–0.85; Table 3, p. 19) are lower at the bottom of the range than the class-mean reliabilities typically seen with 20 or more respondents. The drop in 2014 clinical practice (teacher variance 0.007; Table 3) matters most here. That literature would be a stronger benchmark than a single G-study, and it offers established explanations for low aggregate agreement, such as short exposure to a teacher (a clinical-practice class of volunteers taught for two weeks) *(own knowledge / interpretive)*.

*Placement in adjacent fields.* The paper is at home in economics of education and in U.S. educational measurement. It draws little on educational and school psychology, where the German three-dimensions tradition (Klieme, Praetorius, Kunter) and the Dutch ICALT tradition have produced cross-national reliability and invariance evidence for both observation and student perception, some of it in middle-income countries. It also makes little use of organizational and sociological work on how evaluators actually rate, which explains why practitioner raters are lenient or compress scores for relational and motivational reasons. Examples include Kimball & Milanowski (2009, *Educational Administration Quarterly*), Grissom & Loeb (2017), and qualitative studies of evaluation implementation (own knowledge). The paper itself suggests coaches may be "narrowing and raising scores to encourage teachers" (p. 21), a hypothesis that literature has examined directly. Finally, on the LMIC side, the paper cites the World Bank and RISE instrument-development work (Bruns et al., 2016, 2018; Filmer et al., 2022; Molina et al., 2018; pp. 9, 21) but not the LMIC coaching literature, where observation data are used operationally to target support. Cilliers et al. on South Africa and Kraft, Blazar, & Hogan (2018) on coaching generally are examples (own knowledge). That literature is where the paper's intended use, allocating coaching, actually happens.

*Minor internal inconsistencies that affect how the literature comparison is summarized (checkable).* The Introduction's clinical-practice ranges have relative and absolute swapped: "0 to 0.71 (0–0.75)" on p. 3 against relative 0–0.75 and absolute 0–0.71 on p. 15 and in Table 2. Together with the 44/45 count and the two single-rater survey ranges, this means the abstract- and introduction-level summaries of how this paper relates to prior work should be checked against Tables 2–3 before being quoted.

*Limits of this assessment.* I could not see Supplemental Appendices A and B, including Table A.1, on which the paper's entire quantitative comparison with prior work rests. I verified these items against primary sources or abstracts during the review: Hill et al. (2012) design; Ho & Kane (2013) design and findings; Praetorius et al. (2014) main finding; the existence and content of Bartanen & Kwok (2021), Molina et al. (2020), and Chaplin et al. (2014); and the Schweig (2014) abstract. Other literature claims are from memory and flagged as such. Some may be imprecise, particularly exact scales, years, and which studies report formal G-coefficients as opposed to other reliability indices.

---

### Writing Review

**Rating:** Weak (moderate confidence)

At the sentence level the paper reads cleanly and is well organized: the Introduction lists five numbered findings, the Analysis section explains the G-theory designs in plain terms, and the Results section points readers to specific rows, panels, and x-coordinates. The problem is that too many of the numbers in the prose do not match the exhibits they cite. Two exhibit rows are mislabeled ("single observation" when the values are for the two-lesson design), Figure 2 cannot be reproduced from Table 3, a range in the Introduction is swapped, and several qualitative claims ("varied little," "more variable," "all but one") are contradicted by the tables. The main qualitative conclusions still hold. Wide variation across conditions, a single-lesson mean close to the literature's, and diminishing returns to extra lessons and raters all survive. But a reader should not quote any specific number from the prose without first checking it against Tables 2 and 3.

**Strengths:**

- The Introduction (pp. 2–3) gives the reader a clear map: five numbered findings, each with concrete coefficient ranges and pp. gains, plus a section roadmap.
- The paper explains G-theory well for non-specialists. Design notation such as d×(l:t) and t×d×o is spelled out in words on pp. 8–9, and pp. 12–14 explain each variance component in plain language.
- Tables 1–3 have a sensible structure. Rows and columns follow the design (context × rater assignment × year), and the tables report teacher counts, SDs of the teacher effect, SEMs, and both relative and absolute coefficients. The SDs of the teacher effect are the square roots of the teacher variance components, and they check out in every column of Tables 2 and 3.
- Table 3's coefficients are internally consistent. Using the paper's Eqs. 4–7 with n_d = 7 and n_r equal to the "Average number of raters" row, I reproduce all eight coefficients (0.33/0.29, 0.58/0.57, 0.85/0.70, 0.59/0.36) and all four SEMs.
- Figure 1 agrees with Table 2. Its curves at 2 lessons/occasions match Table 2's coefficients, and its values at 1 lesson match the single-observation figures quoted on p. 15. I recomputed these from the Table 2 components and checked them against pixel readings of the plotted markers.
- The Results prose tells readers where to look, e.g., "on the third row from the bottom" (p. 15) and "the y-coordinate of the blue lines at two lessons" (p. 17). That habit is what makes the mismatches below checkable.
- The later text is appropriately cautious about non-random rater assignment (p. 17; Discussion p. 21) and about unmodeled facets (p. 22).

**Weaknesses:**

- **Rows in Tables 2 and 3 are mislabeled.** The Table 2 rows "SEM of a single observation" and "Reliability of single observation" actually report the operational two-lesson/two-occasion design (n_l = n_o = 2). The text's own "single observation" figures (p. 15: range 0–0.61, mean 0.39) are the n = 1 values. So the paper uses "single observation" in two incompatible senses, sometimes on the same page (pp. 15, 18).
- **Figure 2 does not match Table 3.** At the operational rater counts, panels A and B of Figure 2 read roughly 0.10 below and above Table 3's coefficients, respectively. The survey D-study text on pp. 18–20 follows the figure, while the Introduction's survey increments (p. 3) follow Table 3. As a result, the survey D-study numbers in the Introduction and the Results disagree.
- **The Introduction swaps a range.** p. 3 gives the clinical-practice ranges as relative 0–0.71 and absolute 0–0.75. Table 2 and p. 15 give relative 0–0.75 and absolute 0–0.71.
- **Several qualitative claims contradict the tables:**
  - "varied little from one year to the next" (p. 17), although same-coach relative reliability goes from 0.34 to 0.52;
  - surveys "more variable" in clinical practice (p. 19), although the clinical-practice ranges are no wider than the school-year ranges;
  - adding raters helps "in all but one of the scenarios" (p. 19), although all four Figure 2 curves rise.
- **The Figure 1 narrative (p. 17) mixes reference points.** It describes relative-error levels "when each teacher is rated twice" using the one-lesson values, but describes absolute-error levels using the two-lesson values. It also cites panels and x-positions that do not match the claimed increments.
- **Exhibit labels contradict the text on how school-year surveys were administered.** Tables 1 and 3 and Figure 2 label both 2014 and 2015 as "All different students per occasion/lesson." The text (pp. 9, 19) says 2014 surveyed the same students twice, and the abstract and p. 19 use that 2014-vs-2015 difference to explain the drop in survey reliability.
- **Counts do not reconcile.**
  - Table 1 reports 28 teachers for 2015 school-year surveys; Table 3 reports 25.
  - The literature benchmark is "44" estimates on pp. 3 and 15 but "45" on p. 6.
  - Clinical-practice observation analyses total 80 teachers in 2014 (30 + 25 + 25) and 100 in 2015 (37 + 43 + 20). But only 32 and 45 teachers entered in those cohorts (p. 9), and each teacher was observed on two lessons, each by one rater (p. 8). The text never explains how this adds up.
- **The abstract speaks more strongly than the body.** It says reliability "depends upon" context and rater assignment, while the body says rater assignment was not random and differences should not be read as properties of rater types (pp. 17, 21). It attributes survey variation to a change in the students sampled, which the per-occasion design cannot isolate (see Detailed Commentary). It also gives the 0–0.75 range without noting that the 0 is a variance component truncated at zero in one 25-teacher cell.
- **Key benchmark material is not in the main text.** The headline comparison to prior research rests on Table A.1 in Supplemental Appendix A, which I could not access. Caveats are scattered across pp. 12, 17, and 22 rather than collected in a limitations section.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Must read:** "Procedure" (pp. 7–9, especially "Clinical Practice" and "School Year"), Table 1, Table 2, Table 3, and the caveat paragraph at the top of p. 17 on non-random rater assignment. These carry the paper.
- **Can skim:** most of "Prior Research" (pp. 4–5, general CTT/G-theory background; but read the Table A.1 summary on pp. 5–6), "Context" (pp. 6–7, Argentina macro statistics), and the equations on pp. 12–14 if you already know G-theory.
- **Read Table 2's "Reliability of single observation" and "SEM of a single observation" rows as two-lesson (or two-occasion) values.** The true one-lesson relative coefficients are the p. 15 figures (0–0.61, mean 0.39), or the x = 1 points in Figure 1. Likewise, read the p. 15 confidence intervals as intervals for a two-lesson average. A true one-lesson SEM, recomputed from Table 2, runs from about 0.26 to 0.48.
- **Trust Table 3 over Figure 2 and the survey D-study prose on pp. 18–20.** Table 3 is internally consistent; Figure 2 panels A–C are not consistent with it.
- **Use Table 2 or p. 15 for the clinical-practice ranges, not p. 3.**
- **Treat the survey D-study as extrapolating downward from current practice.** Its "10 students" baseline sits well below the operational 18.5–25.5 respondents (Table 3, last row). The coefficients in Table 3 are already the roughly 20-student values.
- **Check the n for each coefficient before quoting it.** Each clinical-practice "same coach" estimate averages per-coach G-studies of only about 4–5 teachers each (30/7 and 37/8 teachers per coach; p. 8, Table 1). The "0" coefficients come from a teacher variance estimated as negative and set to zero (Table 2, col. 5).
- Do not rely on the p. 17 claim that coefficients "varied little" year to year, or the p. 19 claim that clinical-practice surveys were "more variable." Read the year-to-year and context-to-context spreads directly from Tables 2 and 3.
- The 44-vs-45 benchmark count, and whether the "remarkably close" 0.39 mean includes the single survey estimate, cannot be resolved without Supplemental Appendix A.

  *See the correction note in the synthesis: both counts are right.*

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Organization and navigability.* The paper follows a conventional arc and is easy to navigate. The Introduction's five numbered findings are the most useful reader aid, but they are also where the most number drift occurs: the Introduction appears to have been written against a different version of the tables or figures than the Results. The Results section has two parallel halves (observations, surveys), each covering G-study levels, then context and rater comparisons, then D-study curves, then costs. That parallelism helps. Methodologically important caveats are scattered: ceiling effects and range restriction on p. 12, non-random assignment on p. 17, unmodeled facets on p. 22. The Discussion has no dedicated limitations section. The paper's main external benchmark (Table A.1, 15 prior G-studies) lives in a supplement I could not access, so the headline "remarkably close to the mean of 0.39" comparison (pp. 3, 15) cannot be checked from the article alone.

*The "single observation" labeling problem.* This is the most consequential exposition issue because it affects the paper's central quantity. I recomputed each Table 2 coefficient from the reported variance components using Eqs. 3, 5, 6, and 7 (n_d = 6), and Eqs. 9 and 10 for the school year. With n_l = n_o = 2, the recomputed values reproduce every entry in the "Reliability of single observation" rows (relative 0.34, 0.52, 0.75, 0.75, 0, 0.51, 0.63, 0.66; absolute 0.29, 0.33, 0.71, 0.71, 0, 0.48, 0.59, 0.44). They also reproduce every entry in the "SEM of a single observation" row (0.254, 0.184, 0.265, 0.248, 0.340, 0.295, 0.256, 0.193). With n = 1, the relative coefficients are 0.22, 0.36, 0.61, 0.60, 0, 0.36, 0.47, 0.51: range 0–0.61, mean 0.39. That is exactly what p. 15 (and p. 3) call the "single-observation" coefficients. So p. 15's calculation is right, but it contradicts the row label of the very table it cites.

The same page then uses the Table 2 SEM row ("The SEM for a single observation ranges from 0.184 to 0.340") to build confidence intervals. Those intervals therefore describe a two-lesson average, not one observation. A true one-lesson SEM would run from about 0.26 to 0.48, and the worst-case interval would span roughly half the 1–5 scale rather than "about a third." Two smaller points about these intervals, both interpretive: the intervals are framed as uncertainty about a teacher's location on the score scale, which is an absolute interpretation, yet they use the relative-error SEM, which is smaller than the absolute-error SEM. And the best-case arithmetic is slightly off: 3 ± 1.96 × 0.184 gives [2.64, 3.36] (width 0.72), not [2.65, 3.35] (width 0.70). The worst-case and survey intervals are arithmetically correct. Table 3 uses the same "single observation" row labels for what are whole-class, roughly 20-respondent values; its note calls this the "SEM of a single survey," which is at least defensible.

*Figure 2 vs. Table 3.* Table 3 is internally consistent: its coefficients follow from its components at the "Average number of raters." Figure 2 is not consistent with Table 3. Reading the plotted markers (pixel-measured, about ±0.02):

- **Panel A (clinical practice 2014):** about 0.24 relative and 0.21 absolute at 20 raters. Table 3 col. 1 gives 0.33/0.29 at 19.7 raters.
- **Panel B (clinical practice 2015):** about 0.69 relative and 0.67 absolute at 18.5–20 raters. Table 3 col. 2 gives 0.58/0.57 at 18.5 raters.
- **Panel C (school year 2014):** about 0.87 relative and 0.745 absolute at 24 raters. Table 3 col. 3 gives 0.85/0.70. This is a smaller gap and I label it probable rather than certain.
- **Panel D (school year 2015):** matches Table 3.

Panel B's curve happens to match what one gets by swapping Table 3's rater:teacher and residual components (0.506 and 0.270). That suggests, but does not prove, a transposition in either the figure or the table.

The practical consequence is that the survey D-study prose disagrees with itself. The Results (pp. 18–20) read their levels and gains off Figure 2: relative 0.15–0.55 at 10 clinical-practice students, +9 pp in 2015. The Introduction's "7 to 10 pp" and "6 to 10 pp" gains from 10 to 15 students (p. 3) match a recomputation from Table 3 (+6.8/+9.9 relative, +5.6/+9.6 absolute), not the figure (about +5/+9 relative, +4/+9 absolute). Similarly, the school-year gain from adding five students is "6 to 9 pp" on p. 3 but "5 to 8 pp" on p. 20. There is also a framing issue: the D-study narrative starts from 10 students, while ExA already surveys about 18–26 per class (Table 3). A casual reader will take the 10-student coefficients as current practice.

*Figure 1 narrative (p. 17).* Figure 1 itself is consistent with Table 2, but the prose describing it is not:

- "Between 0.2 and 0.6 when each teacher is rated twice" matches the one-lesson points (0.22–0.61). At two lessons, the values are 0.34–0.75 (panels A–D, F).
- "Between 0.4 and 0.5 [school year] when each teacher is rated twice" matches one occasion (0.47, 0.50). At two occasions they are 0.63 and 0.66.
- The "+8 pp from adding an occasion" is the gain from two to three occasions. So the paragraph pairs one-occasion levels with two-to-three gains.
- In the same paragraph, the absolute-error levels (school year 0.4–0.6) are read correctly at two occasions.
- The clinical-practice absolute claim, "between 0.3 and 0.7 ... same coach or a different peer (panels A–B and E–F)," fits no reading. At two lessons those panels show 0.29, 0.33, 0, and 0.48. The next sentence points to "four lessons in panels A, E, and F" as evidence for the gain from adding one lesson, and panel E is flat at zero.

A reader who tries to follow these panel-and-coordinate pointers will not land on the stated numbers.

*Qualitative claims that outrun the tables.*

- **"Varied little" (p. 17).** The paper says that apart from different-peer observations, coefficients "varied little from one year to the next." Table 2 shows same-coach relative reliability rising from 0.34 (2014) to 0.52 (2015), and school-year absolute reliability falling from 0.59 to 0.44. The Discussion (p. 22) itself stresses "significant year-on-year variation."
- **"More variable" (p. 19).** Clinical-practice surveys are said to be "lower and more variable" than school-year surveys. The spreads are 0.25 vs. 0.26 (relative) and 0.28 vs. 0.34 (absolute), so the school year is, if anything, more variable.
- **"All but one" (p. 19).** Adding raters is said to help "in all but one of the scenarios," but every Figure 2 curve increases. The phrase appears to be carried over from the observation section, where Figure 1 panel E is genuinely flat.
- **"Apparent stability" (p. 19).** The same paragraph refers to "the apparent stability in reliability estimates" for surveys, which contradicts the section's opening claim that surveys "vary widely."

*Abstract fidelity.* The abstract states the question and method accurately. On findings:

- **Observation range.** "From 0 to 0.75" is accurate for the relative coefficient. However, the 0 is a boundary estimate from one 25-teacher cell whose teacher variance was estimated as negative and set to zero (Table 2, col. 5). The 0.75 comes from a same-rater design, where rater effects are plausibly absorbed into the teacher component (interpretive).
- **"Depends upon ... rater assignment configurations."** This is causal-sounding language the body walks back. The body says rater assignment was not random, so differences are "further evidence that reliability is sensitive to design features, rather than ... a property of rater types" (p. 21).
- **Survey variation "coinciding with a change in the students sampled across occasions."** This is loosely true but is the least well-supported sentence in the abstract, for four reasons (interpretive, though grounded in checkable table values):
  1. School-year surveys are analyzed as separate per-occasion d×(r:t) designs (pp. 9, 14). Whether the same students answered on both occasions therefore does not enter those coefficients directly.
  2. The 2014 to 2015 drop in Table 3 comes from teacher variance (0.094 to 0.020), not rater or residual variance (0.222/0.399 vs. 0.213/0.369).
  3. The design change is confounded with year.
  4. Clinical-practice surveys vary just as much (0.33 vs. 0.58) with no design change.
- **Omissions.** The abstract does not mention the small per-condition samples (20–48 teachers, and about 4–5 per coach-level G-study) or the large standard errors that the body repeatedly asks readers to keep in mind.

*Tables and figures.* Beyond the problems above:

- Table 1's column (5), headed "Raters per lesson/occasion," contains assignment descriptions rather than counts.
- Table 1's note says "one per coach" G-studies "in all cases," including the survey rows, where the split is by occasion.
- Table 3's school-year header reads "per lesson," while Table 1 and Figure 2 say "per occasion."
- Figure 2's x-axis starts at 5 and neither figure marks the operational n (2 lessons/occasions; about 18–26 students). Readers cannot see where current practice sits on each curve.
- Figure 1 panel E (a flat line at zero) carries no note that it reflects a truncated variance component.
- The text says D-study Eqs. 11–12 let n′_l and n′_r vary, but as typeset the prime appears only on the last term (p. 14). The text cites "Equations 5 to 7" where Equations 3–7 are meant (p. 14).
- The abstract misspells "reliability" as "reliabilty."

*Density.* At 27 pages, including about 6 pages of references, the paper is not long, but the numbers are dense and repeated. Nearly every range appears in the Introduction, again in the Results, and again inside the figure narrative. That triples the opportunity for drift and, as shown above, drift occurred. A time-constrained reader gets the most value from Tables 1–3 plus pp. 8–9 and p. 17.

- The school-year mean relative coefficient is given as 0.64 (pp. 3, 15). The table values average 0.645, and unrounded recomputation gives 0.65.

- Observation ranges and means on pp. 2 and 15 (0–0.75, 0–0.71; 0.48/0.42 clinical practice; 0.52 school-year absolute).
