---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper offers a rare, fully reported set of G-studies and D-studies of classroom observations and Tripod-style student surveys that a Teach for All affiliate in Argentina ran for formative purposes (about 100 teachers, 2014–2015). Its most useful contributions are descriptive and practical. It records what reliability looks like when practitioners run the process with a 1-hour rater training, and it shows how much extra lessons or respondents would help. The headline claim that its estimates are "comparable to those from research in high-income countries" is weaker than it looks. In 7 of the 8 observation analyses, rater variance is never part of the error term, the one configuration that does count it produced reliabilities of 0 and 0.51, and the prior-study benchmark sits in an appendix I could not see. The paper is best cited as evidence that reliability depends on the design, not as evidence that practitioner ratings match research-grade reliability.

**Strengths:**

- **A real gap in setting.** The paper studies observations and surveys run by an organization for its own operational purposes in an upper-middle-income country. The design is candidly framed as a joint "stress test" of whether research-setting reliability evidence travels (p. 9). The authors also say plainly that they cannot tell which of several simultaneous differences drives any similarity or difference with prior work (country, instrument, raters, quality assurance; p. 21). That framing is honest and suits a first descriptive study.
- **Transparent, reproducible reporting.** Tables 2 and 3 (pp. 16, 19) report every variance component with its standard error. I recomputed the published coefficients from those components using Eqs. 3–10, and they match: for example, Table 2 col. 1 gives ρ² = 0.34 and Φ = 0.29, and col. 8 gives 0.66 and 0.44. The single-observation relative coefficients reported in the text (range 0 to 0.61, mean 0.39; p. 15) also reproduce exactly when n_l or n_o is set to 1. Few papers in this literature publish enough detail for readers to run their own D-studies.
- **A documented practitioner baseline.** The paper records conditions that research G-studies rarely capture: a single 1-hour training session followed by rating one practice lesson (pp. 7–8); an in-house composite protocol drawn from five U.S. instruments with "no back-translation or piloting" (p. 11); rater assignment driven by logistics (pp. 8–9); and scores used to allocate coaching support (p. 7). This makes the paper a useful reference point for what "operational" measurement looks like in LMIC teacher-development programs.
- **Practical D-study guidance, with costs in view.** Moving from two to three clinical-practice lessons raises relative reliability by 6–9 pp (p. 17; I verified this against Table 2, cols. 1–4 and 6). Adding a third school-year occasion adds about 8 pp (p. 17; verified for cols. 7–8). Gains shrink after that (Figure 1, p. 18). The paper's cost reasoning is useful to practitioners: adding lessons during clinical practice is cheaper than during the school year, and adding survey respondents is nearly free when every attending student is already surveyed (pp. 17–18, 21).
- **Appropriately cautious Discussion.** The authors treat rater-type differences as "evidence that reliability is sensitive to design features, rather than as a property of rater types" (p. 21). They warn that D-study recommendations are imprecise (p. 22) and recommend "limited randomization and double scoring" (p. 22), which is the most actionable advice in the paper.

**Weaknesses:**

- **The headline comparison with high-income research does not compare like with like.** (a) Checkable facts: every lesson or occasion had exactly one rater, so rater stringency could not be estimated (pp. 8–9). The same-coach analyses were run separately for each coach and then averaged (pp. 8–9; Table 1 note, p. 10). (b) My interpretation: in the same-rater configurations (Table 2, cols. 1–4 and 7–8), the coefficients measure reliability across lessons for a fixed rater. Rater-by-teacher effects are part of the teacher ("true") variance rather than the error. The only configuration in which rater differences count as error is "different peer per lesson," and its relative coefficients are 0 and 0.51 (Table 2, cols. 5–6, p. 16). The match of means (0.39 here vs. a mean of 0.39 and median of 0.38 in prior studies; pp. 3, 15) averages 8 very different estimates, one of which is exactly 0. The comparison is also against a benchmark in Supplemental Table A.1, which I could not see. The number of prior estimates is inconsistent across the text: 44 on pp. 3 and 15, and 45 on p. 6. So the more tempting inference, that practitioner observations with a 1-hour training are about as reliable as research-grade observations, is not something this design can test. Rater error is exactly the error that research-setting training and certification aim to reduce.
- **The peer-versus-coach contrast may be partly an artifact of how the data were analyzed.** (a) Fact: coaches were analyzed per coach, while peers, who each observed only one teacher, were pooled (p. 8). Peer ratings average higher than coach ratings (Table 1, col. 8, p. 10: coach means 2.48 and 2.60; peer means 2.92–3.59). (b) My interpretation: per-coach G-studies remove each coach's leniency from the teacher variance. The pooled peer analysis leaves each peer's leniency inside the teacher variance. That alone could produce the much larger teacher variance for same-peer ratings (0.210 and 0.180) than for same-coach ratings (0.034 and 0.037) (Table 2, cols. 1–4). The paper lists range restriction, pairing, and coach score-narrowing as possible mechanisms (p. 21), but not this one.
- **Much of the "wide variation" may be estimation noise.** Samples are 20–48 teachers per column (Table 1, p. 10). The clinical-practice coach analyses average across 7–8 coaches covering 30–37 teachers, so each coach-level G-study has roughly 4–5 teachers (Table 1, p. 10; my division). Key teacher-variance estimates are about as large as their standard errors: 0.034 (0.028) and 0.037 (0.030) in Table 2, cols. 1–2, and 0.007 (0.006) in Table 3, col. 1. The 0 reliability in Table 2, col. 5 is a negative variance estimate set to zero. No intervals are reported for the coefficients themselves (p. 12). The paper says as much (pp. 15, 17), but the abstract presents the spread "from 0 to 0.75" as a substantive finding.
- **The survey coefficients answer a narrower question than their labels suggest.** Each survey analysis is run within one occasion. Lesson, occasion, and class are not error facets (pp. 8–9), so the coefficients describe how reliable a single class-occasion's average is, not a teacher's score in general. The abstract's link between lower 2015 school-year reliability and the change in which students were sampled across occasions is carefully worded ("coinciding"). Still, a within-occasion design cannot directly show that the sampling change caused the drop (Table 3, cols. 3–4: 0.85 vs. 0.59). The comparison with prior survey research rests on a single estimate (Schweig, 2014: 0.16; p. 6).
- **External validity is asserted more than shown.** The evidence comes from one organization, one province, two years, and about 100 teachers (p. 9). The teachers are fellows in an alternative-certification program, the observation protocol is a bespoke composite rather than CLASS or FfT (p. 11), and the data are from 2014–2015, more than a decade before publication. The case for relevance to the 60-organization Teach for All network rests on similar procedures (pp. 2, 7), not on data from other members.
- **Reporting slips that affect what gets cited.** (1) Table 2's row "Reliability of single observation" actually reports coefficients for the two-lesson or two-occasion design. It reproduces with n_l or n_o = 2 and matches Figure 1 at x = 2. The true one-lesson values run from 0 to 0.61 (p. 15). (2) The Results text describes clinical-practice relative reliability "when each teacher is rated twice" as 0.2–0.6 and school-year reliability as 0.4–0.5 (p. 17). Those ranges match Figure 1 at one lesson or occasion, not two. (3) The single-student survey coefficients are given as 0.03–0.25 on p. 3 but 0.02–0.35 on p. 18. My recomputation from Table 3 gives about 0.03–0.25. (4) Figure 2, panels A–B (p. 20) do not match what Table 3's components imply for clinical-practice surveys. At the observed respondent counts, the table gives about 0.33 (2014) and 0.58 (2015), while the figure shows roughly 0.25 and 0.7 at 20 raters (my reading of the plot). (5) The 2015 school-year survey sample is 28 teachers in Table 1 and 25 in Table 3.
- **The novelty claim leans on the LMIC setting more than on practitioner raters.** The paper itself cites prior U.S. work using non-research observers or administrative data (Glazerman et al., 2011; Whitehurst et al., 2014; Ho & Kane, 2013). My own understanding, not verified from the paper, is that Ho & Kane (2013) studied observations by school administrators and peers. What is new is the combination of an LMIC setting, operational administration, and formative use. I did not independently audit whether earlier G-studies exist in Latin American contexts, and the authors' "one of the first" (abstract; p. 21) is suitably hedged.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Cite it for:** a documented case showing that observations run by practitioners in a middle-income nonprofit, with minimal rater training, gave two-lesson, same-rater G coefficients of 0.34–0.75 (Table 2, p. 16). Describe these as reliability across lessons for a fixed rater.
- **Cite it for:** the caution that reliability depends heavily on the design and on who is assigned to rate whom. In particular, the one configuration that counts rater differences as error (different peer per lesson) gave 0 and 0.51 (Table 2, cols. 5–6). That is the weak spot operational systems should expect.
- **Cite it for:** the shape of the D-study returns. A third lesson or occasion adds about 6–9 pp, with sharply diminishing returns after that (Figure 1, p. 18). Adding survey respondents from the same class is often cheap (p. 21).
- **Cite it for:** a transparent template. It publishes the full variance components and explains the designs that operational data typically produce (nested, one rater per lesson). The authors state that data and code are provided (p. 22). I could not verify this because the supplementary materials were not available to me.
- **Do not cite it for:** "practitioner observations are as reliable as research observations." In most analyses rater error is not measured, the prior-study benchmark (Table A.1) is in an appendix I did not see, and a match in means over 8 very different estimates is a coarse test.
- **Do not cite it for:** "peers are more reliable raters than coaches" or "coaching-context observations become more reliable once teachers are in schools." Both contrasts are confounded by non-random assignment, cohort differences, and, for peers vs. coaches, the different analytic treatment. The authors themselves disclaim reading them as properties of rater types (pp. 17, 21).
- **Do not cite it for:** Table 2's "single observation" figures as single-lesson reliabilities. They are two-lesson or two-occasion values. The single-lesson mean is 0.39 (p. 15).
- **Do not cite it for:** precise D-study gains for clinical-practice surveys. Figure 2, panels A–B do not reconcile with Table 3.
- **Read "practitioners should conduct their own reliability analyses" with care.** The paper's own precision problems suggest that a local G-study with about 30 teachers and one rater per lesson may be too noisy to act on. The better-supported recommendation is the paper's narrower one: build in double scoring and some randomization so that rater variance can be estimated (p. 22).
- **Open questions:** How large is rater variance under practitioner conditions, and does a brief training cost much compared with certification? Answering that requires double-scored lessons. How stable are these estimates with more recent data and across other Teach for All members? And how valid are these scores, for example in predicting student learning? The paper explicitly does not validate them (pp. 9–11).

**Detailed Commentary:**

*What is new.* The paper's genuinely new element is its setting. Operational, practitioner-administered, formative observation and survey data from a middle-income country are analyzed with full G-theory decompositions. The authors describe the prior G-study literature as confined to high-income countries: 15 studies, 87% of them in the United States (p. 5; the underlying Table A.1 was not available to me). If that description is accurate, this paper adds a new data point from a new kind of setting. It does not add new methodology. The G- and D-study machinery (Eqs. 1–15, pp. 12–14) is standard (Brennan, 2001), which is appropriate for this genre. The survey instrument is a translated Tripod (p. 11), so the survey results are the closest like-for-like comparison with U.S. work. The observation protocol, by contrast, is ExA's own blend of CLASS, FfT, TAL, PLATO, and MQI (p. 11). Comparing its reliability with CLASS or FfT estimates is therefore a comparison across instruments, and the paper's framing of instruments as belonging to "similar instrument families" (p. 9) does not fully close that gap.

*The gap between the best-supported claim and the most quotable one.* The abstract offers two quotable claims: reliability is "comparable to those from research in high-income countries," and "practitioners should conduct their own reliability analyses." The first rests on a match of means (0.39 vs. 0.39; p. 15). My main concern for readers is what that match compares. In a G-study, the universe of generalization is defined by the facets the design treats as error. With one rater per lesson, and a single rater per teacher in the same-coach and same-peer configurations, the published coefficients describe consistency across lessons as seen by one rater. A rater's persistent leniency toward a particular teacher counts as true-score variance. That is a known way hidden facets inflate generalizability coefficients. The paper's p. 22 limitation says unmodeled facets are "absorbed into residual variance." For facets held constant within teacher, such as the assigned rater here, the more worrying case is absorption into teacher variance instead. The one configuration where rater variation is part of the error term, different peer per lesson, is the weakest (0 in 2014, 0.51 in 2015; Table 2, cols. 5–6, p. 16). So the data support a cautious reading: under practitioner conditions, reliability across lessons for a fixed rater looks similar to published research estimates, and reliability across raters is unknown and may be low. That is a useful finding, but it is not the claim the abstract makes. The inference that minimal training did not cost much reliability is untested, because the error that training targets is rater error.

The second abstract claim is closer to the evidence but needs a caveat. The paper shows that its estimates vary across contexts, years, and rater configurations (Table 2). How much of that variation is real rather than sampling noise is unclear. With 20–48 teachers per column (Table 1), per-coach analyses of roughly four to five teachers each in clinical practice, and teacher-variance estimates close to their standard errors (Table 2, cols. 1–2; Table 3, col. 1), much of the spread could be noise. That cuts both ways for the recommendation. It supports not borrowing benchmarks, but it also suggests that one local G-study of similar size may not tell a practitioner much. The paper's own later advice, repeated analyses plus double scoring and some randomization (p. 22), is what makes local analyses informative. Readers who pass on the "do your own analysis" message should pass on that condition too.

*Generalizability.* The authors are careful in the body of the paper (pp. 9, 21–22) and more expansive in the introduction and data sections. There they argue that membership in Teach for All makes the results "potentially relevant beyond the specific context" (pp. 2, 7). The actual sample is narrow: about 100 alternative-certification teachers from one organization in the Province of Buenos Aires (p. 9), observed in 2014–2015, largely by coaches and fellow novices. The findings will travel best to similar programs, meaning nonprofit fellowship models that use observations and student surveys to allocate coaching. They will travel less well to public-system evaluation, where raters are principals or supervisors, stakes are higher, and instruments are usually established protocols. The paper does not claim otherwise, but its practitioner-facing framing invites broader use than the data support.

*Standing in the literature.* As far as I can judge without the appendix, this is now a useful public reference for the variance structure of practitioner-run observations and student surveys in a Latin American setting. The survey results in particular add to a U.S. literature with, by the paper's own count, one prior single-rater estimate (p. 6). It is not the best evidence on rater reliability among practitioners in general. Designs with multiple raters per lesson are needed for that question, and this paper cannot address it by construction. The natural follow-on work is clear, and the paper sets it up well. Double-scored, partially randomized rater assignments in one or more Teach for All members would estimate the missing rater facet. Replications with current data and established LMIC instruments would test stability. Validity work would link these scores to student outcomes or to decisions about coaching support.

*Reporting slips.* Several small inconsistencies matter mainly because they could spread through citation. The first is the Table 2 row label: "Reliability of single observation" actually shows two-lesson or two-occasion coefficients. I confirmed this by recomputing the coefficients from the variance components, and the values match Figure 1 at two lessons or occasions. The others are the mismatched descriptions of Figure 1 on p. 17, the two different single-student survey ranges (p. 3 vs. p. 18), the Figure 2 A–B mismatch with Table 3, the 28 vs. 25 teacher count, and the 44 vs. 45 prior-estimate count. None of these changes the paper's qualitative story. Together they suggest readers should take specific numbers from Tables 2–3 and their own recomputations rather than from the prose.

*Bottom line.* This is a modest, carefully hedged, and transparent contribution on an important practical question for LMIC teacher-development programs. It deserves citation as a descriptive case and a methodological template. Its most quotable line, reliability "comparable to" high-income research, rests on a comparison the design cannot fully support, because rater variance is missing from most of its error terms. Its best-supported message is narrower: reliability under operational conditions is design-dependent, lesson-to-lesson consistency within a rater can be moderate, and cross-rater reliability is the unmeasured risk. That calls for double-scored local designs rather than borrowed benchmarks. Supplemental Appendices A and B, including Table A.1 and the promised data and code, were not available for this review. I cannot assess the quality of the prior-study benchmark or verify the replication materials.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The paper's core computational layer holds up. Every generalizability coefficient, standard error of measurement (SEM), and teacher-effect SD in Tables 2 and 3 can be recomputed exactly from the printed variance components with the stated equations, and the Figure 1 D-study curves regenerate as well. The authors also say they deposited data and code "with this paper." Three gaps weaken the evidence trail. First, the main text gives no locator or software statement for that deposit. Second, the analytic samples cannot be rebuilt from the description: teacher counts across rater configurations exceed cohort sizes under the stated two-lesson, one-rater design. Third, Figure 2 (panels A–B) and its narration do not match Table 3. Verification therefore depends on the supplement and deposit, which this review could not inspect.

**Strengths:**

- **The coefficients can be recomputed from the tables.** Using the Table 2 variance components (p. 16) with Eqs. 3, 5, 6, 7 and 9, 10 (pp. 13–14), I reproduced all 16 reported coefficients in cols. 1–8 to two decimals at the as-administered design (n_l or n_o = 2, n_d = 6). I also reproduced all 8 SEMs and SDs. Using Table 3 (p. 19) with Eq. 4 and the reported "Average number of raters" as n_r (n_d = 7), I reproduced all 8 coefficients and 4 SEMs. Details are in the commentary.
- **The single-observation summary checks out.** The text reports single-observation relative coefficients of 0 to 0.61 with a mean of 0.39 (p. 15, Results). Setting n_l = n_o = 1, I get 0.22, 0.36, 0.61, 0.60, 0, 0.36, 0.47, and 0.50, which gives a range of 0–0.61 and a mean of 0.39.
- **Figure 1 regenerates.** The D-study curves for observations (p. 18) match Eqs. 11, 13, 14, and 15 applied to Table 2 at every lesson count I checked. The Introduction's D-study increments (p. 3) also reproduce: +6 to +9 pp relative for a third lesson, and +8 pp for a third school-year occasion.
- **Designs and estimands are clearly stated.** The notation d×(l:t), d×(r:t), and t×d×o is explicit for each analysis (pp. 8–9; Table 1, col. 7, p. 10), with full score decompositions (Eqs. 1, 2, 8) and error-variance formulas. The estimator (REML, p. 13), the delta-method SEs (p. 12; Table 2 and 3 notes), and the rule that negative components are set to zero (Table 2 and 3 notes) are all named.
- **Precision is reported.** Every variance component comes with an SE (Tables 2–3), and each analysis has a teacher count, number of lessons or occasions, domain count, and elemental mean and SD (Table 1, p. 10).
- **Data and code sharing is claimed.** The paper says it "made the datasets and code from our analyses available with this paper" (p. 22, Discussion). A supplement is referenced (p. 23), and Supplemental Appendix B is said to link to the full observation protocol (p. 11).

**Weaknesses:**

- **The deposit cannot be located from the main text.** The sharing claim (p. 22) gives no repository, URL, DOI, file list, license, or access terms. The main text also has no data availability statement, no software or package statement, and no note on permission from the data provider (Enseñá por Argentina) or on de-identification of teacher-level data. "Supplemental material for this article is available online" (p. 23) is the only pointer.
- **The analytic samples cannot be rebuilt as described.** Clinical practice is described as two lessons per teacher with "one rater scoring each lesson" (p. 8), and a teacher takes part in clinical practice only in the year hired (p. 7). Yet the three 2014 clinical-practice configurations contain 30 + 25 + 25 = 80 teacher-analyses from a 32-teacher cohort. The 2015 configurations contain 37 + 43 + 20 = 100 from a 45-teacher cohort (Table 1, col. 3, p. 10; cohort sizes p. 9). "Some teachers are included in multiple analyses" (p. 9) means many teachers had more than two scored lessons or more than one rater per lesson. The paper does not say how lesson–rater records were chosen for each configuration, which conflicts with its own "one rater per lesson" statement.
- **The exclusion rule is unspecified.** "Some teachers were observed fewer times than the rest, so we dropped them" (p. 9) gives no threshold, no counts dropped per analysis, and no flow from 100 teachers to the Table 1 samples.
- **The per-coach and per-rater aggregation is ambiguous.** The paper reports "the average result across coaches" (p. 8; Table 1 note) over 7 or 8 coach-level G-studies in clinical practice and 3 or 4 rater-level studies in the school year. It never says whether variance components or coefficients were averaged, how teachers were weighted, or how the SEs of averaged components were formed. With 30 teachers and 7 coaches (Table 1), each coach-level REML fit rests on roughly 4 teachers. The same ambiguity applies to how the two school-year survey occasions were combined into Table 3, cols. 3–4, and to how "Average number of raters" was averaged: across teachers, across occasions, arithmetic or harmonic.
- **Estimator details are missing or in tension.** No software, estimation routine, or convergence handling is reported. Components "estimated as negative were set to zero" (Table 2 note) suggests an unconstrained or ANOVA-type estimate, which sits oddly with REML (p. 13). The paper does not say whether models were refit after truncation. The headline coefficients themselves carry no SEs or intervals; only the components do.
- **Figure 2 conflicts with Table 3.** Panels A–B of Figure 2 (p. 20) cannot be regenerated from Table 3. They also disagree with Table 3's own coefficients at the reported rater counts. The Results narration on pp. 19–20 follows the figure, while the Introduction (p. 3) follows Table 3.
- **Labels and cross-references are inconsistent.**
  - The Table 2 and 3 rows labeled "Reliability of single observation" and "SEM of a single observation" actually hold two-lesson or two-occasion (and ~20-student) values, not the one-lesson definition given on p. 15.
  - Table 3, col. 4 lists 25 teachers, but Table 1 lists 28 for the same analysis.
  - The benchmark set is described as "44 estimates" (pp. 3, 15) and as "45 reliability estimates" (p. 6).
  - The single-rater survey range is "0.03 to 0.25" on p. 3 and "0.02 to 0.35" on p. 18.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- **Trust the Table 2–3 coefficients as arithmetic.** They are exact functions of the printed components. The open question is whether the components are right, and that cannot be checked without the data and code.
- **Get the deposit before relying on specific numbers.** Obtain the replication materials from the journal's supplement page or the corresponding author. Confirm that they include (a) the lesson-, rater-, and coach-level identifiers needed to rebuild each Table 1 sample, (b) the exclusion code, and (c) the per-coach, per-rater, and per-occasion G-study outputs and the averaging step.
- **Read Figure 2 panels A–B and the Results survey numbers from Table 3 instead.** At 10 students, Table 3 components imply relative coefficients of about 0.21 (2014) and 0.43 (2015) for clinical-practice surveys, not the 0.15 and 0.55 in the text (p. 20). Panel C is also modestly off; panel D matches.
- **Recompute before citing an SEM or confidence interval.** The "single observation" SEMs and 95% intervals on p. 15 (0.184–0.340; [2.65, 3.35] to [2.33, 3.67]) are for the two-lesson average. By my computation, one-lesson SEMs from Table 2 run from about 0.26 to 0.48. The survey SEMs on p. 18 (0.119–0.173) are for the mean over about 19–26 students, not a single survey response.
- **Treat the rater-configuration contrasts as least verifiable.** The same peer versus a different peer versus the same coach (Table 2, cols. 1–6) is the comparison where sample construction is most opaque. Without the selection rule for lesson–rater pairs, a reader cannot tell whether the three groups are comparable subsets.
- **Do not lean on the prior-literature benchmark without the supplement.** The mean of 0.39 and median of 0.38 across prior estimates (p. 15) depend on Table A.1, which is not in the main text and is counted inconsistently (44 vs. 45).

  *See the correction note in the synthesis: both counts are right.*

**Detailed Commentary:**

*Availability.* The Discussion says: "We have also made the datasets and code from our analyses available with this paper" (p. 22). That is a stronger commitment than "available upon request," and it deserves credit. The data come from a non-profit's operational feedback system, and the surveys were anonymous (p. 9). Nothing in the setting obviously bars sharing de-identified teacher-level data. However, the main text gives no repository name, DOI, URL, file manifest, or license. It also has no statement of software or version, no data-use or permission statement from ExA, and no description of how teacher, coach, or peer identities are protected in the shared files. The only pointer is the generic "Supplemental material for this article is available online" (p. 23). I could not inspect the supplement or any deposit, so I cannot confirm that the data and code exist, run, or reproduce the tables. My rating assumes the deposit is real but unverified.

*Specification transparency.* The model side is well documented for a G-theory paper. Each design is named and justified: lessons nested in teachers in clinical practice, occasions crossed in the school year, and raters nested per occasion for surveys (pp. 8–9). The linear decompositions are written out (Eqs. 1, 2, 8, pp. 12–13), as are the relative and absolute error variances and coefficients (Eqs. 3–7, 9–10) and the D-study versions (Eqs. 11–15, p. 14). The unit of analysis is stated: the G-studies decompose domain scores, with domains treated as a random facet (p. 12). Table 1's means and SDs are instead at the "teacher-by-lesson-by-rater-by-item" level (Table 1 note), so they do not describe the analyzed data directly. Three estimator details are unstated: the software, the handling of truncation, and the delta-method parameterization. The delta method implies the components were estimated on a transformed scale, such as log-SD, but the paper does not say so. Several components are printed as "0 (0)": Table 2, col. 5 teacher and domain × teacher; col. 7 occasion. A replicator cannot tell whether these are REML boundary estimates or negative estimates that were truncated after the fact. That distinction affects the other components if the model was not refit.

*Sample construction.* Here a replication would have to guess most. Table 1 (p. 10) gives the counts but not the path to them. The sampling section (p. 9) reports 100 teachers: 23, 32, and 45 by cohort. It says only that teachers "observed fewer times than the rest" were dropped and that configurations are analyzed separately. The arithmetic in the Weaknesses section is a checkable fact: 80 clinical-practice teacher-analyses from 32 teachers in 2014, and 100 from 45 in 2015. Under the stated two-lesson, one-rater design (p. 8), a teacher could fall into only one configuration. The counts therefore imply additional scored lessons or multiple raters on some lessons. Neither is described. If multiple raters sometimes scored the same lesson, a partially crossed design would have allowed estimation of rater stringency. The paper says that estimation was impossible (p. 8). My interpretation is that the underlying data are richer than described, and that some unreported rule selected two records per teacher per configuration. That rule is the single most important undocumented step. The school-year counts (48 of 55 eligible in 2014; 35 of 77 in 2015; cohorts from p. 9) and survey counts are feasible. For 2015 school-year observations, though, the drop from 77 eligible to 35 analyzed is large, and no reason is given beyond the generic exclusion sentence.

The coach- and rater-level aggregation is the second key undocumented step. The paper runs separate G-studies "for each coach (seven in 2014 and eight in 2015)" and reports "the average result across coaches" (p. 8). Likewise for school-year raters (p. 9; Table 1 note). Four things are not specified: (i) whether variance components or coefficients were averaged; (ii) whether averages are weighted by teachers; (iii) how SEs for the averaged components in Table 2 were derived; and (iv) how coaches with very few teachers were handled. Averaging nonlinear coefficients and computing coefficients from averaged components generally give different answers. My recomputation (below) shows that the printed coefficients equal the coefficients implied by the printed averaged components. That is consistent with "average the components, then compute," but the text never says so. With about 4 teachers per coach in clinical practice (30 / 7, Table 1), each coach-level teacher-variance estimate is extremely noisy. The aggregation rule is therefore material, not cosmetic. The same question applies to the school-year surveys, run as separate G-studies per occasion (2[d×(r:t)], Table 1, col. 7) and reported in a single column of Table 3. Table 3, col. 4 also lists 25 teachers where Table 1 lists 28, which suggests a different sample or an occasion-specific count. Neither table explains the difference.

*Recomputations: the tables regenerate.* Table 2, col. 1 (p. 16) reports σ²_t = 0.034, σ²_d = 0.117, σ²_l:t = 0.086, σ²_dt = 0.059, and σ²_res = 0.142. With n_l = 2 and n_d = 6, Eq. 3 gives relative error 0.086/2 + 0.059/6 + 0.142/12 = 0.0648. Then ρ² = 0.034/(0.034 + 0.0648) = 0.345, against 0.34 reported. SEM = √0.0648 = 0.254, against 0.254 reported. Φ = 0.034/(0.034 + 0.0648 + 0.117/6) = 0.288, against 0.29 reported. The same procedure reproduces cols. 2–6 exactly (0.52/0.33, 0.75/0.71, 0.75/0.71, 0/0, 0.51/0.48) along with every SEM and SD row. For the school-year t×d×o columns (Eqs. 9–10, n_o = 2), I obtain 0.632/0.588 for col. 7 (reported 0.63/0.59) and 0.662/0.436 for col. 8 (reported 0.66/0.44).

For Table 3, col. 1 (p. 19), take σ²_t = 0.007, σ²_r:t = 0.198, σ²_dt = 0.014, σ²_res = 0.296, σ²_d = 0.020, n_r = 19.7 (the reported average), and n_d = 7. Eq. 4 gives relative error 0.198/19.7 + 0.014/7 + 0.296/(7·19.7) = 0.01420. Then ρ² = 0.330, Φ = 0.291, and SEM = 0.119, against 0.33, 0.29, and 0.119 reported. Cols. 2–4 also match: 0.577/0.565, 0.849/0.695, and 0.586/0.358, against 0.58/0.57, 0.85/0.70, and 0.59/0.36. The means in the text also follow from the tables:

- clinical-practice observations: 0.48 relative, 0.42 absolute
- school-year observations: 0.64–0.65 relative, 0.52 absolute
- clinical-practice surveys: 0.46 relative, 0.43 absolute
- school-year surveys: 0.72 relative, 0.53 absolute

All are on pp. 15 and 19. The p. 15 confidence intervals follow from 3 ± 1.96 × SEM, with trivial rounding in the best case ([2.64, 3.36] vs. [2.65, 3.35]).

*Labeling.* The table rows headed "Reliability of single observation" and "SEM of a single observation" reproduce only at n_l = 2 (or n_o = 2), and for surveys at n_r equal to the full average class count. They do not reproduce at the one-lesson, one-rater definition the text uses on p. 15. The coefficients the text calls single-observation values (0–0.61, mean 0.39, p. 15) reproduce only at n = 1. A reader who takes the row labels at face value, or the p. 15 phrase "SEM for a single observation," will overstate single-lesson precision. By my computation, one-lesson SEMs are 0.26–0.48, not 0.18–0.34. On the survey side, my single-rater values of 0.03, 0.07, 0.25, and 0.07 match the Introduction's "0.03 to 0.25" (p. 3). They do not match the Results' "0.02 to 0.35" (p. 18).

*Recomputations: the figures.* Figure 1 (p. 18) regenerates. For example, panel A: my Eq. 11/13 values run from 0.22/0.20 at one lesson to 0.59/0.44 at eight lessons, matching the plotted points. Panel H runs from 0.50/0.29 to 0.86/0.68, also matching. The narration of Figure 1 on p. 17 has one oddity. It says the clinical-practice relative coefficient "is between 0.2 and 0.6 when each teacher is rated twice," and the school-year coefficient is "between 0.4 and 0.5 when each teacher is rated twice." Those ranges match the one-lesson or one-occasion points (0.22–0.61; 0.47–0.50), not the two-lesson points (0.34–0.75; 0.63–0.66). The stated increments (+6 to 9 pp and +8 pp from adding a third lesson or occasion) are correct from two to three.

Figure 2 (p. 20) is where regeneration fails. From Table 3 via Eq. 12, clinical-practice panel A should read about 0.21 relative at 10 raters, 0.33 at 20, and 0.47 at 40. Panel B should read about 0.43, 0.60, and 0.74. The plotted points are approximately 0.15, 0.24, and 0.35 in panel A and 0.55, 0.70, and 0.82 in panel B (my visual readings). The figure also contradicts Table 3's own coefficients at the reported rater averages. Panel A at about 20 raters shows roughly 0.24, while Table 3 reports 0.33 at 19.7. Panel B at about 18.5 raters shows roughly 0.68, while Table 3 reports 0.58. Panel C sits modestly above my values (about 0.77 vs. 0.74 at 10 raters). Panel D matches (about 0.39 and 0.28 vs. my 0.40 and 0.28). The Results narration follows the figure: "between 0.15 and 0.55 with 10 students" and absolute "between 0.14 and 0.54" (p. 20). The Introduction's survey increments instead follow Table 3: +7 to 10 pp relative and +6 to 10 pp absolute in clinical practice, and +6 to 9 pp and +4 pp in the school year (p. 3). My Table-3-based values are +6.8/+10.0, +5.6/+9.6, +5.8/+8.5, and +4.1/+3.9 pp. I cannot tell which set of variance components produced Figure 2, and I do not speculate about the cause. The checkable fact is that Figure 2's clinical-practice panels are not generated by the components printed in Table 3.

*Overall judgment.* This is an interpretive call. The central quantitative claims in the paper are the ranges and means of the generalizability coefficients and the observation D-studies. They are internally regenerable from the printed variance components, which is more than many G-theory papers allow. That, together with a stated data-and-code deposit, supports "Adequate" rather than "Weak." Two things keep the paper from "Strong." First, sample construction and per-coach aggregation are not documented well enough for an independent team to rebuild the variance components without the authors' code. Second, the exhibits contain internal inconsistencies that a reader should resolve against the tables. These are the Figure 2 mismatch, the mislabeled "single observation" rows, the 25 vs. 28 teacher count, the 44 vs. 45 benchmark count, and the conflicting single-rater survey ranges. My confidence is limited mainly because Supplemental Appendices A–B and the deposit were unavailable. They may resolve several of the sample-construction and software gaps noted here.
